A news wire tuned for mass tort teams. Each firm gets its own private copy, built around the litigations it signs and the firms it watches.
h: What it watches · What it sets aside · How it reads · Four starting desks · Terms of the pilot
x: Tools Mass Tort Wire A news wire tuned for mass tort teams. Each firm gets its own private copy, built around the litigations it signs and the firms it watches. Free pilot · Copies set up on request AI has made the news harder to stay ahead of. A ruling posted in the morning is rewritten across dozens of sites by noon and buried by the next day. One story runs under a dozen headlines, and the rulings and settlements that matter get lost among the copies. I built Mass Tort Wire for my own desk to keep up with that pace. Each time it opens, it gathers the news on the litigations I follow and the firms I watch. It folds the rewrites of a story into one item and sets aside the stories that would waste the morning. Through March 2027 I am setting up free copies for a small number of plaintiff firms, policyholder-side teams, and the companies that serve them. On the wire now What it watches Your litigations. The wire follows each litigation you track under every name the press uses for it. Talc also catches “baby powder,” and asbestos also catches “mesothelioma.” The firms you watch. The wire follows each firm you name for verdicts, filings, leadership appointments, sponsorships and deals. A firm’s own blog can feed the wire directly. When the firm’s post and the press story about it cover the same event, the two appear as one item. The trade and legal press. Reuters and Law360 run on every copy. The update pages on Lawsuit Informer and the analysis on Lawsuit Intelligencer arrive the day they publish. Informer also gathers its update pages on one current mass tort cases board , which shows where each case stands with the newest court entries first. What it sets aside I read the raw feed every day and write a filter for each story type that wastes a reader’s morning. Stock-market coverage of defendants stays off the wire. A documentary about the 1982 Tylenol poisonings stays out of the Tylenol litigation. A hockey player who shares a firm’s name stays out of that firm’s news. A story that names none of your litigations or firms goes behind an OFF-TOPIC line, one tap away. How it reads The wire runs in a phone or desktop browser and installs to a home screen like an app. It groups stories by day and marks each one NEW for 24 hours after it arrives. Two tabs sort the feed. News Wire carries everything. AI Wire follows AI in the courts and in legal work, along with the AI safety and policy news that tends to reach the courts next. A third tab holds whichever desk a firm runs. A firm that tracks law firm investment, MSO or funding topics gets Deal Wire there. A policyholder-side team gets Risk Wire, for coverage litigation and the exposures that drive it. A copy can also carry a Docket tab for the dockets a firm signs. The tab checks those dockets four times a day and lists each new order, ruling and settlement, with a link to the filing. Appearances, summonses, short-form complaints and clerk entries stay off the list. Four starting desks Litigation desk. The active consumer mass torts and the national plaintiff firms, for a firm that signs cases. Deal desk, buyer. MSO and private equity news, the platforms doing deals, and the docket events that price an inventory: bellwether results, Daubert rulings, settlement programs. Deal desk, seller. The same deal coverage, plus the state rules on nonlawyer ownership and fee sharing, and the firms that have already taken investment. Risk desk. Coverage litigation read from the policyholder’s side. It covers denials and bad faith verdicts, and the exclusions carriers are writing into D&O and technology errors and omissions policies. It also follows allocation and exhaustion fights in long-tail exposures, and the recalls and enforcement actions that become coverage disputes before they become settlements. Every desk is a starting point. A firm adds its own litigations and firms on top, and I adjust any copy the same day a firm asks. Terms of the pilot A copy is free through March 31, 2027. It lives at its own address with the firm’s name at the top. The firm gets a read-only key to share across its team, and only I can change the copy. The firm’s topic list stays in that copy and is never shared with another firm. The wire counts opens, scans and story clicks so I can see whether it earns its place on a firm’s screen. It records nothing else. It may carry one sponsor line later, from a company that serves the plaintiff bar. A law firm will never be a sponsor. The pilot covers the news copy and a Docket tab for up to three dockets the firm signs. Before the pilot ends, I will send each firm the terms for keeping its copy after March 31, and the firm decides then. A firm that stops owes nothing, and its copy comes down. Request a copy Email editor@lawsuitintelligencer.com with three lines: your firm, the litigations you sign, and the firms you watch. A deal team or a coverage team can name the desk instead: buyer, seller or risk. Name up to three dockets you want watched, and the copy comes with a Docket tab for them. I set up the copy and reply with its address and key, usually the same day. Request a copy Mass Tort Wire is built and maintained by David Meldofsky , editor of Lawsuit Intelligencer.

t: The Preparation Does Much of the Negotiating
d: Elliott Portnoy, who advises private equity sponsors on law firm MSO transactions, on why the plaintiff-side deals that close at higher multiples were won a year before the first sponsor meeting.
e: Interview · The Business of Plaintiff-Side Law
h: On what sixty combinations taught him · On the firms that close at higher multiples · On the firms that wait · On building the advisory team · On compliance · On what sponsors bring beyond capital
x: Interview · The Business of Plaintiff-Side Law The Preparation Does Much of the Negotiating Elliott Portnoy, who advises private equity sponsors on law firm MSO transactions, on why the plaintiff-side deals that close at higher multiples were won a year before the first sponsor meeting. By David Meldofsky · September 23, 2026 · 5 min read Private equity’s route into plaintiff-side practice runs through the management services organization. A sponsor buys into an MSO that runs the firm’s marketing, intake, technology and finance, and the firm pays the MSO a management fee for those services. The lawyers keep the practice and every professional judgment in it. What a firm owner should have in place before a sponsor looks at the books is the subject of this interview. Elliott Portnoy was the founding Global CEO of Dentons, the world’s largest law firm, where he led more than 60 law firm combinations. He now advises private equity sponsors on investments in the legal sector, including MSO transactions involving plaintiff-side firms. I put one question to him in writing: what separates the deals that come together well from the ones that struggle. His answer puts most of the outcome in the firm’s own hands, a year before any sponsor meeting. The firms that close at higher multiples arrive with case data a sponsor can underwrite, an administrative services agreement already drafted, and partners who agreed to the direction months earlier. Compliance, he says, is the most critical element in every deal he works on, and he tells firm leaders to be wary of any sponsor who treats it lightly. His answer runs below in full. The section headings are mine. On what sixty combinations taught him Meldofsky: From your seat advising private equity sponsors, what separates the plaintiff-side MSO deals that come together well from the ones that struggle, and how should law firm leaders prepare? Portnoy: I advise private equity sponsors investing in the legal sector and other professional services. That work covers MSO and ABS transactions, AI-native law firms, alternative legal service providers, and legal technology companies. Before that, I spent many years at Dentons as its founding Global CEO. I led more than 60 law firm combinations that brought together about 12,000 lawyers and 10,000 non-lawyer professionals across 85 countries. The lesson I carry into my private equity work is that most of the value in a transaction depends on preparation and integration. That applies directly to MSO transactions and matters most for platforms that plan to grow through add-on acquisitions and will need to bring together talent, systems, technology, process, and compensation across firms. On the firms that close at higher multiples I often see the same pattern. The transactions that close most smoothly and at higher multiples are typically those where the law firm did much of the hard work well before speaking with bankers or sponsors. The financials hold up to a quality-of-earnings review. The firm has years of clean case data that a sponsor can use to build a cash forecast and underwrite with confidence. Case-cost advances are tracked apart from operating expense. The firm can produce its KPIs on request, including churn, advertising and lead-generation costs, signed cases by source, cost per signed case, intake conversion, average fee by case type, time to resolution, and case realization. The MSO structure exists, not only on paper. Law firm leaders have decided which functions move to the MSO and have an administrative services agreement in place or at least drafted. The partners have been part of the conversation for months or longer and support the direction. That readiness shows up in the valuation. On the firms that wait Law firms that wait for a sale process to start this work end up paying for it. So do firms whose leaders decide not to discuss outside capital with their own partners. Sponsors see this quickly. Data arrives late. Answers change between meetings. Partners raise objections in diligence that should have been settled a year earlier. Leaders worry about how the partnership will receive the news and learn late in the process that the partnership agreement contains obstacles no one anticipated. The timeline stretches, the multiple comes down, and sometimes the process breaks. On building the advisory team Law firm leaders should build their advisory team early, and it should include more than a banker. A banker who knows legal services is invaluable for running a competitive process and setting value. Leaders also need deal counsel who have closed MSO transactions and ethics counsel who know the rules in every state where the firm practices. They need accountants who can prepare the firm for a quality-of-earnings review, a valuation firm to support the management fee, tax advisors to structure the proceeds, and a compensation expert to design a deferred compensation plan built for the MSO. The best advisors have done this many times, and firms that bring them in a year ahead of a process get better terms. On compliance Compliance is the most critical element in every deal I work on. The ethics rules and related guardrails are the starting point for the structure, and nothing should come anywhere near the line. Every professional judgment stays with the lawyers. The management fee is priced based on the services the MSO delivers and is supported by an independent valuation. The sponsors I work with insist on this. They plan for an eventual sale, and the next buyer will test the structure. A law firm leader who senses a sponsor is paying too little attention to ethics and compliance should be wary. On what sponsors bring beyond capital When law firm leaders arrive unprepared, they often underestimate what private equity brings beyond capital. Many sponsors have owned and scaled businesses in accounting, consulting, communications, physician and dental practices, insurance, and veterinary care, and a growing number have done so in the legal sector. They bring operating partners who have built marketing, intake, technology, recruiting, and finance functions many times, including within law firms. In a plaintiff practice, that experience goes straight to the largest cost lines. Sponsors bring deep knowledge of media buying, digital advertising, and SEO. They know how to build the data systems that connect each advertising dollar to signed cases and fees. Law firm leaders who miss this tend to choose a sponsor based on headline price alone and fail to consider the sponsor’s operational capabilities. The law firm leaders who do best have their structure, numbers, advisors, and partners in place before the first meeting. Those conversations move quickly. Their preparation does much of the negotiating for them. Elliott Portnoy was the founding Global CEO of Dentons, the world’s largest law firm, and now advises private equity sponsors on investments in the legal sector, including law firm MSO transactions. Portnoy answered one question in writing. His answer appears in full and as written. The section headings are the editor’s, and one sentence was repunctuated. The figures on the Dentons combinations are Portnoy’s own. — DM Disclosure: The author holds referral relationships with plaintiff-side firms in mass tort litigation, as described in the editorial standards . No firm, sponsor, or transaction is discussed in this interview. No payment was exchanged in either direction. David Meldofsky is a California-licensed attorney and the editor of Lawsuit Intelligencer. He is also the founder of Lawsuit Informer and Lawsuit Center .

t: The MSOs Are Hungry Right Now
d: Frederick Shelton, who represents law firms selling to legal MSOs, on why he tells founders not to wait a year, why he calls the multi-year EBITDA earnout the bottom of the deal-structure food chain, and what an owner owes the lawyers who hold no equity.
e: Interview · The Business of Plaintiff-Side Law
h: On the year sponsors ask for · On the management fee · On what a sponsor actually brings · On the lawyers with no equity · On contingency-fee revenue and the earnout · On AB 2305 · On Arizona’s ABS and the California firm
x: Interview · The Business of Plaintiff-Side Law The MSOs Are Hungry Right Now Frederick Shelton, who represents law firms selling to legal MSOs, on why he tells founders not to wait a year, why he calls the multi-year EBITDA earnout the bottom of the deal-structure food chain, and what an owner owes the lawyers who hold no equity. By David Meldofsky · October 13, 2026 · 11 min read Three weeks ago in this series, Elliott Portnoy described the plaintiff-side MSO deal from the sponsor’s side of the table. The firms that close at higher multiples, he said, did their preparation a year before the first meeting. This interview is the view from the other chair. Frederick Shelton represents the law firm in these transactions, and he agrees with Portnoy on almost every step of the preparation. He disagrees about the calendar. Shelton is Chief Executive Officer of Shelton & Steele, a national advisory firm that handles law firm mergers, acquisitions, and sales to legal management services organizations. He also writes on the legal industry. Last October, under the headline The Legal MSO: The Next Billion-Dollar Industry , he told American Lawyer readers that legal MSOs would become a billion-dollar industry. A year and one reported $700 million deal later, he has moved from forecasting the market to selling firms into it. Portnoy’s clients put up the money. Shelton’s clients take it, and the buyer pays Shelton. Shelton & Steele spent 30 years in lawyer recruiting and law firm mergers, where it represented the partner or the practice group and the hiring firm paid the fee. It has carried that fee arrangement into MSO deals. The firm advocates for the seller, and the MSO pays it. The law firm pays nothing. Shelton says the sponsors accept the arrangement for the same reason the Am Law firms did. “They just wanted qualified candidates and firms,” he wrote in an email. “It’s the same now with MSOs. They actually like having us on deals because we provide the teams of attorneys, accountants, etc., so that founders have the confidence to actually do the deals.” A sponsor who gets a year of preparation gets cleaner numbers to underwrite and a firm that has already invested in the process. A seller who goes to market while buyers outnumber sellers gets the terms that scarcity brings. Each man is describing the calendar that suits his side of the table, and the owner reading both should price that in. I sent him seven questions in writing. His central claim is that sponsors need deals now and qualified firms are scarce. A prepared firm, he says, should sell into that scarcity instead of waiting out a year-long readiness program. His firm turns down most of the MSOs it screens. He wants owners to reserve equity for the partners who will run the firm after the founders leave. He treats a multi-year earnout keyed to EBITDA as the structure most likely to turn a strong valuation into a weak check. His answers run below, edited for clarity. The section headings are mine. On the year sponsors ask for Meldofsky: Sponsors tell owners to have their case data, services agreement and partners in place a year before a process. From the firm’s side, what does that year cost an owner, and which parts are worth doing before the firm knows whether it will sell at all? Shelton: That advice is based on sound reasoning and experience with investors. Right now, some horrible deals are being walked into by partners who didn’t prepare properly and didn’t think they needed experienced advisors, attorneys and consultants. However, some of the best deals that will ever be written are closing right now because the MSOs are hungry. They’re under a lot of pressure to get deals in the door, so we’re working on deal structures with very strong valuations, favorable terms and zero earnouts. When a firm has partner alignment, strong growth and a compelling story, we can get them educated, prepared and ready to enter the market in less than a week. We spend hours educating founders about how these deals work and what to expect. We introduce them to deal and ethics counsel almost immediately. We almost always introduce the founding partners to fractional CFOs who clean up and normalize the financials and, particularly for plaintiff firms, help organize the operating data behind the numbers, including case inventory, attrition, average fees, acquisition costs and time to resolution. Later in the process, we introduce Quality of Earnings specialists who independently test and validate that financial story so the founder walks into diligence with numbers that can withstand scrutiny by the MSO. We also bring in consultants to educate founders about the key performance indicators that actually drive the business, and to help them identify where better systems, technology or capital could improve profitability. Those are things a firm should be doing whether it ever pursues an MSO deal or not. But they don’t all have to be completed before entering the market. Strong, understandable financials matter from the beginning. A formal Quality of Earnings analysis can come later in the process and does not need to be the price of admission just to start talking to MSOs. While I understand why experienced sponsors would think in terms of a year, I disagree with the idea that every firm needs to wait, especially in a sizzling hot market. The MSOs are hungry right now . They need deals and they’re under pressure to get them. It’s about supply and demand. Right now, the demand is high for qualified law firms and the supply is low. The Charlesbank deal for Wood Smith was reported at an 18X multiple. While I doubt that number will survive, it demonstrates why being a nimble market adapter is important. This is especially true for our small to mid-sized firms. Yes, preparation matters, but so does first mover advantage. We help firms prepare quickly so they can capitalize on this high demand, low supply market. On the management fee Meldofsky: The management fee is where the ethics rules and the sponsor’s return meet. When you negotiate that fee for a firm, what are you protecting the owner against, and which fee structures cause trouble in later years? Shelton: The safer standards are properly structured fair market value, cost plus and flat fee arrangements. What we don’t want is something that even remotely resembles fee sharing. That’s why we introduce founders to expert legal MSO attorneys who focus on exactly this issue. They can prevent a management fee from turning into fee sharing in disguise. On what a sponsor actually brings Meldofsky: Sponsors say they bring operating expertise in marketing, intake and finance. Where have you seen that promise hold up in a plaintiff firm, and where has a firm ended up paying a management fee for services it already ran well? Shelton: The best MSOs don’t walk in assuming everything needs to be fixed. They first look for what a firm is already doing well. For example, one of our founders brought in business by speaking at conventions. Now that she doesn’t have to deal with all the administrative burdens, the MSO is sending her to double the number of conventions and paying for her to have better placement. That law firm just had its three most profitable months in 30 years of practice. Once the MSO operators infuse resources and capital into what works, they look for what could be improved, or what they call “levers.” Maybe that’s AI handling client intake in twelve languages, 24/7. It could be automating much of the medical records process, increasing marketing spend or moving beyond traditional SEO toward better results from AI searches. They’ll also look to add profitable attorneys or even acquire firms. Where it goes wrong is when some finance bro in a Patagonia vest arrives with a predetermined playbook to “professionalize” a successful law firm. We’ve turned down about 60 of the 70-plus MSOs we’ve interviewed, because we believe that an attorney who has built a successful law firm probably knows what they’re doing. On the lawyers with no equity Meldofsky: Owners usually roll equity into the MSO. Associates and non-equity partners usually get nothing. Who speaks for the lawyers with no equity in the negotiation, and what should an owner build into the structure for the people who will still be there after the owner exits? Shelton: I love this question because I have an article coming out on this subject soon. One of the biggest mistakes we see is spending enormous amounts of time negotiating on behalf of the founding partners and forgetting about the key people who helped get the firm where it is, or who will help do so in the future. We’ve worked with clients on deals that carve out part of that back-end MSO equity for current and future partners and C-levels. That rewards the next generation and, yes, creates some pretty effective golden handcuffs. Another concept to understand is that as the value of the equity in the legal MSO grows, slices can continue to be carved out for future personnel. Every founding partner should also ask about the possibility of annual equity grants, wherein the MSO awards the founding partners additional equity to minimize the dilution of the pool as more people join. If the founding partners get rich at closing while everybody else gets nothing, they may have completed a great transaction that will result in the extinction of their firm in the long run. On contingency-fee revenue and the earnout Meldofsky: A sponsor underwrites a plaintiff firm on its case inventory. What do sponsors get wrong about contingency-fee revenue, and how does that mistake show up in the valuation or the earn-out? Shelton: The biggest mistake MSOs make is treating contingency-fee revenue like predictable recurring revenue that should be constant. An MSO that doesn’t understand litigation, might assume that if the most recent twelve months hasn’t been that strong, the business has become less valuable. They might ignore a history of year-after-year double-digit growth, because they can’t think outside the private equity box. A plaintiff firm can have extraordinary case inventory and lower EBITDA simply because several large cases haven’t resolved yet. The value didn’t necessarily disappear. It’s just a timing issue. If an MSO can’t understand that, the founders should question whether the MSO will be a good partner. This is why we always spend over an hour with each MSO asking about their experience in legal or legal-adjacent industries and vetting them to make sure they “get it” when it comes to the profession of law. This isn’t health care or accounting. It’s an entirely new breed. That’s why we’ve turned down so many of the MSOs we’ve interviewed. There are a lot of MSOs out there. There aren’t a lot of good ones. If a partner senses that an MSO doesn’t understand all this, they may want to reconsider entering into a relationship with them. If another suitable MSO isn’t currently available for a particular practice area, sometimes the better option is simply to wait until profitability normalizes rather than accept a weak valuation. It’s also one reason we strongly avoid multi-year EBITDA earnouts. I call them the bottom of the deal-structure food chain. A founder can do everything right, then lose millions because cases resolved in year three instead of year two. That’s how a $50 million valuation can end up turning into only $20 million of money actually received by the founding partners. If the sponsor understands plaintiff law, the structure should recognize that volatility rather than transferring all of the timing risk back to the founder. On AB 2305 Meldofsky: California’s AB 2305 takes effect for contracts signed on or after January 1. It voids any term that lets a sponsor influence client selection, fees, settlement or strategy, and puts statutory damages on both the lawyer and the investor. Colorado and Illinois went further and reached the MSO fee itself. What in a standard services agreement no longer survives, and what should a firm owner now refuse to sign? Shelton: This is exactly why deal structure and specialized ethics counsel matter. The trend is pretty clear. States are scrutinizing all things MSO nowadays, and they’re drawing hard lines around who controls the practice of law and what constitutes fee sharing. Again, the tried and true structure is fair market value, cost plus or flat fees. The lawyers must retain control over clients, fees, cases, strategy and settlements. If these are in place, both the MSO and the firm are sound. On Arizona’s ABS and the California firm Meldofsky: Arizona lets a sponsor own a law firm outright through an Alternative Business Structure, while an MSO leaves the lawyers holding the practice and the sponsor holding the services company. California has cut off fee-sharing with out-of-state ABSs and put both models under AB 2305. For a plaintiff firm with California cases, which model is still open, and what does the owner keep under each that they give up under the other? Shelton: For a California plaintiff firm, a properly structured MSO remains available. The lawyers continue to own the law firm and, importantly, control the practice of law. Arizona’s ABS model is fundamentally different, because non-lawyers can have an economic interest or decision-making authority in the entity providing legal services. With an MSO, the investor owns the management company, not the law firm. That distinction matters enormously. An ABS permits much more direct investor ownership and integration. MSO structures seem better to us because there is no bar on referral fees. The ABS was innovative. The MSO is inevitable. The first deal we got across the finish line was in Arizona, and it was structured as an MSO. I wrote an article predicting the rise of virtual lawyering a year before COVID hit. I wrote another one predicting AI was going to be the tech game-changer for the practice of law before ChatGPT was released. The American Lawyer quoted me predicting the rise of legal MSOs in May 2024. In July 2025, I wrote in Attorney at Law Magazine that legal MSOs were going to be the structural game-changer for the practice of law. Last October, I predicted in The American Lawyer that they would become a billion-dollar industry. I am more confident in the MSO prediction than I was about virtual lawyering or AI. Frederick Shelton is Chief Executive Officer of Shelton & Steele , which advises law firms on mergers, acquisitions, and transactions with legal management services organizations. He can be reached at fs@sheltonsteele.com . On the Wood Smith figure: in August 2026, PitchBook and the Financial Times reported Charlesbank Capital Partners in advanced talks over an MSO stake in Wood Smith Henning & Berman. The reported valuation was about $700 million. Neither party has announced a deal. The EBITDA multiples in circulation, from 15X to 18X, come from the reporting rather than from the parties. Wood Smith is an insurance defense firm with hourly revenue, so its multiple measures the market’s appetite rather than a comparable for a contingency-fee practice. Shelton’s answer originally said Charlesbank had announced the multiple. The sentence was edited to say the multiple was reported, and he reviewed the change. — DM Shelton answered seven questions in writing and reviewed this piece before publication. His answers are edited for clarity, and the section headings are the editor’s. His client examples, the count of MSOs his firm has screened, and the deal outcomes he describes come from Shelton. So does his account of how his firm is paid. None of it was independently verified. — DM Disclosure: The author holds referral relationships with plaintiff-side firms in mass tort litigation, as described in the editorial standards . Shelton & Steele represents law firms in MSO transactions and is paid by the MSO. No client of Shelton’s, and no firm, sponsor, or pending transaction of the author’s, is discussed in this interview. No payment was exchanged in either direction. David Meldofsky is a California-licensed attorney and the editor of Lawsuit Intelligencer. He is also the founder of Lawsuit Informer and Lawsuit Center .

t: The Fee That Isn’t a Fee
d: Private equity’s path into personal injury law rests on a single undefined word. California and Illinois wrote it into their statutes without saying what it means, and no court has decided where a management fee ends and “indirect” fee-sharing begins.
h: What Texas actually decided · The tell is in the number · California reached for the economics but left a gap · Illinois shows the other failure mode · What I’ll be watching
x: Analysis · Regulation & Legal Ethics The Fee That Isn’t a Fee Private equity’s path into personal injury law rests on a single undefined word. California and Illinois wrote it into their statutes without saying what it means, and no court has decided where a management fee ends and “indirect” fee-sharing begins. By David Meldofsky · May 29, 2026 · 7 min read The short version The MSO structure lets investors own a law firm’s back office and charge the firm a management fee. The whole arrangement turns on whether that fee counts as “indirect” fee-sharing, a term no statute defines. Texas Opinion 706 banned only the percentage-of-revenue version. A fixed fee engineered to equal the firm’s profit reaches the same economics and steps around the rule. California’s AB 931 reached for those economics with the words “directly or indirectly,” but never defined “indirect.” The ban is also written to sunset in 2030, so a patient investor can structure around a rule scheduled to expire. Illinois shows the opposite failure: language broad enough to catch the workaround may also catch ordinary vendors, from e-discovery platforms to court reporters. Read enough deal memos and marketing decks and you notice that the entire private-equity push into personal injury law turns on one word nobody has bothered to define. The word is indirectly . It is the load-bearing term in California’s new fee-sharing ban and in the Illinois bill moving behind it. And it will settle the question everything else hangs on — whether the structure now being sold to plaintiff firms is a legitimate vehicle for outside capital, or a workaround waiting for a test case. The setup is familiar by now. Most states forbid non-lawyers from owning a law firm or sharing in its fees. To get capital in anyway, firms split themselves in two: the law practice stays lawyer-owned, and the back office (marketing, intake, technology, HR) is carved into a separate company, the MSO, that investors can own. The MSO then sells those services back to the firm under a long-term management services agreement, frequently running twenty or thirty years. On paper, lawyers keep the law and investors keep the business. No fee is shared. Nothing is owned that can’t be. That is the theory. The mechanics tell a different story, and the difference is the whole subject. What Texas actually decided In February 2025 the Professional Ethics Committee for the State Bar of Texas issued Opinion 706, the first modern ethics opinion to take MSOs head-on. It is cited constantly, usually as a green light. It is worth reading for what it actually says. The committee considered a non-lawyer-owned company offering a bundle of support services that proposed to charge firms a percentage of their revenue. That, the committee held, is prohibited fee-splitting with a non-lawyer under Rule 5.04(a). And, crucially, it remains prohibited even when the percentage is dressed up as payment for services rendered . Tying the MSO’s compensation to the firm’s legal revenue is the violation. The label on the invoice does not save it. Opinion 706 is genuinely permissive in one respect: it confirms lawyers may hold equity in an MSO and that a properly built MSO can live inside the rules. But the bright line it drew is narrow and formal. It bans a percentage . It says nothing about a fixed fee that has been engineered to capture the same economics by a different arithmetic. The tell is in the number Here is how the fixed fee gets set. Transfer pricing is the intercompany-valuation method multinationals use to shift profit between subsidiaries. As Bloomberg Law reported in its recent survey of the trend, investors now use it to calculate how much value is “transferred” to the MSO, then size their investment off that number. The advisory firm L.E.K. Consulting, writing for investors rather than regulators, offers a worked example with admirable candor: a midsize firm generating $20 million in annual revenue might pay its MSO $18 million a year to run all non-legal operations. Work that forward and the investor’s math appears. The $18 million fee is the MSO’s top line. Subtract what the back office genuinely costs to run, say $8 million, and the MSO clears about $10 million a year. Capitalize that at a platform multiple of six and the entity is worth roughly $60 million. The investor buys a controlling stake against that figure. The valuation exists only because the management fee was set high enough to manufacture it. An $18 million “fair market value” charge against $20 million of revenue is not the price of HR, IT, and a phone system. It is the firm’s profit, relabeled. No one staffing the back office of a $20 million firm believes those functions cost $18 million. That figure is not derived from the cost of services plus a reasonable margin; it is derived from what the firm earns. Strip away the vocabulary and the structure is a ninety-percent revenue share wearing the costume of a flat fee. Texas 706 forbids the percentage and is silent on the costume. That silence is the opening, and everyone in the room knows it. California reached for the economics but left a gap California tried to close exactly this opening, and the way it did so is instructive. Assembly Bill 931, effective for agreements entered on or after January 1, 2026, bars California lawyers and firms from sharing contingency fees, “directly or indirectly,” with an out-of-state alternative business structure. It is codified at Business and Professions Code section 6156. The penalties are real: $10,000 per violation or three times the client’s actual damages, whichever is greater, plus fees and costs, on top of State Bar discipline. It also carves out genuine flat-fee arrangements not tied to recovery. And it is temporary by design. The statute includes a sunset clause set for 2030, meaning the ban expires automatically that year unless the legislature affirmatively votes to renew it. As written, it reaches only agreements entered during the roughly four-year window before it lapses. The legislature plainly meant to reach past the label and grab the economics; that is what “indirectly” is doing in the sentence. But the statute never defines it. It does not define “indirect” fee-sharing, and it does not define what counts as non-lawyer “decision-making.” So California has enacted a prohibition that points directly at the transfer-pricing fee without telling anyone where it lands. Is a flat management fee, set by valuation to equal a firm’s profit, an “indirect” share of contingency fees? On the words alone, you can argue it either way, and able lawyers are being paid to argue both. The natural place to resolve that would have been litigation, and for a moment it looked like we would get an answer. Two firms operating through an Arizona ABS, Eleos Law and Wisner Baum, challenged the California ban on constitutional grounds. In December 2025, U.S. District Judge Dolly Gee denied their request for a preliminary injunction, finding the state had a legitimate interest in keeping indirect non-lawyer ownership from entering California through cross-border arrangements. The plaintiffs then dropped the case. The statute stands, but it stands untested on its merits as applied to a real management services agreement . The hard question was raised and then withdrawn. It is still sitting there. A second California measure, Assembly Bill 2305, has since advanced to the state senate; it goes after non-lawyer control of legal judgment more directly than the fee-sharing route. Its progress is worth watching precisely because it suggests Sacramento knows the first statute did not finish the job. Illinois shows the other failure mode If California’s drafting was too vague to bite, Illinois illustrates the opposite danger. House Bill 5487 and its senate twin would prohibit an MSO owned or controlled by a private equity group or hedge fund from charging a firm any fee “directly or indirectly based on the fees, revenues, or profits” of the practice. That language is aimed at the same transfer-pricing maneuver, but it is so broad that, as the ethics lawyer Trisha Rich has warned, it could swallow ordinary commerce. Every firm pays its vendors out of revenue. Read literally, the bill reaches document-management platforms, e-discovery providers, even court reporters, and arguably litigation funding itself. Rich’s objection is that the bill has no limiting principle that lets routine operations continue without technically violating it. Between the two states you can see the drafting dilemma whole. Write “indirect” narrowly and the transfer-pricing fee slips through. Write it broadly enough to catch that fee, and you criminalize buying software. Nobody has yet written it in a way that catches the $18-million-on-$20-million arrangement and nothing else. Doing that requires a court or a regulator to articulate the economic difference between paying for services and paying for profit — and so far none has. What I’ll be watching The honest state of the law is this: the MSO structure is neither clearly permitted nor clearly barred in the jurisdictions that matter most to plaintiff firms. Texas blessed a version of it while forbidding the crude form. California aimed at the sophisticated form and missed the strike zone by leaving its key term undefined. Illinois aimed wider and may hit everything. And the one case that could have produced a merits ruling on a real agreement was dismissed before it got there. Three things will tell us which way this resolves. First, enforcement: whether the California State Bar or a plaintiff’s-side opponent ever brings a section 6156 action against a live management agreement and forces a court to define “indirect” against actual deal documents. Second, valuation discipline: whether the management fees in these deals start to look like the cost of services or keep tracking the firm’s profit, because that ratio is the evidence any regulator will reach for first. Third, the 2030 sunset, which hands Sacramento a scheduled occasion to tighten the language, broaden the ban, or let the experiment lapse entirely. That deadline matters more than it first appears. A roughly four-year prohibition sits against management agreements written to run twenty or thirty years. It may bind only the opening seasons of a deal — and an investor with patience can wait out a rule scheduled to expire on its own. Whether it does expire, or gets renewed and hardened, is its own fight to watch. Until one of those happens, every firm signing a thirty-year management services agreement is making a bet on a word. They are betting that “indirectly” means the narrow thing, not the broad thing. In California, they are also betting the ban sunsets before anyone tests it against their deal. And they are placing both bets years before anyone with the authority to settle them has spoken. That is a long time to be exposed on the strength of a definition that does not exist yet. David Meldofsky is a California-licensed attorney and the editor of Lawsuit Intelligencer. He is also the founder of Lawsuit Informer and Lawsuit Center . He holds no ownership interest in any management services organization, alternative business structure, litigation funder, or law firm discussed in this piece.

t: MDL 3026 Finally Has a Jury in the NEC Docket
d: Three federal bellwethers never reached a jury. The fourth is being tried in Chicago now, and what it actually tests is not the epidemiology but whether a better warning would have changed how one NICU fed one infant.
h: Three cases that died at the gate · The state record is not the tailwind it looks like · Warning causation is the variable that prices the inventory · Durnell shows up in formula · What a verdict does
x: Coverage · Product Liability MDL 3026 Finally Has a Jury in the NEC Docket Three federal bellwethers never reached a jury. The fourth is being tried in Chicago now, and what it actually tests is not the epidemiology but whether a better warning would have changed how one NICU fed one infant. By David Meldofsky · August 17, 2026 · 7 min read Updated November 4, 2026, with the Inman verdict, Abbott’s settlement, the plaintiffs’ remand motion and the current case count. The short version Inman v. Mead Johnson & Company, LLC, No. 1:22-cv-03737, is being tried before Judge Rebecca Pallmeyer in the Northern District of Illinois. It is the first case in MDL 3026 to reach a jury and the first federal Enfamil case, with roughly 825 actions pending behind it. The first-wave bellwethers, all Similac cases, ended at summary judgment after the court excluded plaintiffs' causation experts. In Inman the court denied summary judgment in May and preserved the plaintiff's epidemiology testimony, which is why this one is in front of a jury. State juries have produced more than $625 million in plaintiff verdicts, but the appellate math has been moving the other way: the first NEC verdict in the country was reversed in June for instruction error, and a St. Louis jury returned a defense verdict for Mead Johnson on July 2. The Seventh Circuit's July 24 affirmance in Mar v. Abbott is the more important document for anyone holding inventory. It turned on warning causation, not science, and it makes NICU-specific facts the variable that prices a case. Update, November 4, 2026: A unanimous jury returned a verdict for Mead Johnson on August 31. Reuters reported that the jury found Enfamil did not cause the infant’s NEC. It was the first federal jury to hear the plaintiffs’ causation experts. Four federal bellwethers have now ended for the defense, three at summary judgment and one at trial. Mead Johnson says no NEC jury verdict against it remains outstanding, counting two state trial wins and the Watson reversal. Abbott settled before the verdict came in. On August 20 it agreed to pay about $670 million to resolve the Gill case and the NEC claims of roughly 2,000 more infants. Gill is the Missouri case behind the $495 million verdict discussed below, and Abbott’s filing puts that judgment near $600 million with interest. Abbott called the agreements a compromise of disputed claims and not an admission of liability. Its filing says about 1,700 NEC lawsuits remain pending in federal and state courts, covering about 12,700 infants. The federal docket has not shrunk. The Panel’s November 2 report counts 847 actions pending in MDL 3026, up from about 825 when the trial opened. Abbott’s filing does not say how many of the settled claims sit in the MDL. Mead Johnson has said it will keep defending the cases. For the Similac cases Abbott has not settled, the Seventh Circuit’s warning-causation holding in Mar, discussed below, still sets the terms. The next contest is over where the remaining cases are heard. Abbott has asked the court to enter a case management order it proposed. On October 23 a large group of plaintiffs, Alexis Inman among them, opposed that order in the same filing as a motion to remand. Judge Pallmeyer extended Abbott’s deadline to reply to November 6. Her ruling on the motion is the next entry to watch on this docket. The NEC infant formula litigation has been running for four years without a federal jury ever hearing it. That changed this week in Chicago, where Inman v. Mead Johnson is being tried before Judge Rebecca Pallmeyer. She has presided over MDL 3026 since the Panel centralized the preterm infant nutrition cases in the Northern District of Illinois. Roughly 825 cases are pending on the federal docket, with hundreds more in state court. The plaintiff, Alexis Inman, alleges that her son Daniel was born at 29 weeks. In the NICU he moved from fortified breast milk to exclusive feeding with Mead Johnson's Enfamil Premature product. He developed necrotizing enterocolitis, underwent surgery on June 22, 2020, and died the next day. The claims are failure to warn and design defect, the latter resting on the argument that a different carbohydrate formulation was available and safer. Plaintiff-side announcements are calling this the first bellwether trial. It is more precisely the first bellwether to reach a jury. Three earlier bellwethers were tried only in the sense that they were worked up, scheduled, and then lost before openings. Losing before openings is a different fact pattern, and a more instructive one. Three cases that died at the gate The first wave of MDL bellwethers all involved Abbott's Similac. In each, Pallmeyer excluded the plaintiffs' causation experts and granted summary judgment, so no jury heard the evidence. Read against a state-court record that includes a half-billion-dollar verdict, that divergence looks strange until you separate the two questions being asked. State juries were asked whether cow's-milk-based preterm formula causes NEC and whether the manufacturers said enough about it. The federal court was asked, first, whether the expert methodology clears Rule 702, and the answer three times was no. Inman is different for a narrow procedural reason. The court denied Mead Johnson's summary judgment motion in May and preserved the plaintiff's epidemiology testimony. The jury will hear plaintiff experts on causation for the first time in the federal docket. That is the entire significance of the trial date. Everything else being said about it this week is atmosphere. Worth noting for anyone who plans around trial calendars: this case was set for February, then July 6, then mid-August. Three announced dates for one trial is normal in a large MDL and abnormal in the press releases written about them. The state record is not the tailwind it looks like The plaintiff-side numbers are real. A Missouri jury returned $495 million against Abbott in 2024, and that verdict survived appeal. A Cook County jury awarded $70 million to four families in April, roughly $53 million compensatory and $17 million punitive, after a short deliberation. The aggregate across state verdicts is north of $625 million. The erosion is also real, and it is more recent. On June 16 an Illinois appellate court reversed the $60 million Watson verdict against Mead Johnson, the first NEC verdict in the country. The court cited jury instruction error and ordered a new trial. Two weeks later a St. Louis jury returned a defense verdict for Mead Johnson in the Collins case. The only defense verdict that had been vacated for trial misconduct is itself on appeal. A verdict is not money until it survives review, and this docket has now demonstrated that at both ends. Warning causation is the variable that prices the inventory The most consequential ruling of the summer was not in Chicago. On July 24 the Seventh Circuit affirmed dismissal in Mar v. Abbott, one of the original bellwethers. It held that the plaintiff could not show a stronger NEC warning would have changed anything. In the court's account, the treating physicians already understood the risk and had no viable alternative to fortified formula for that infant at that time. That is a learned-intermediary holding with a feeding-practice overlay, and it does not depend on the science being weak. It means the questions that decide a case are hospital-specific and date-specific. Did that NICU have a donor milk program in place. Was maternal milk available in sufficient volume. What did the treating neonatologist know about NEC risk, and what will that neonatologist say in deposition about whether a different label would have altered the feeding order. Firms evaluating NEC inventory on gestational age and diagnosis alone are underwriting a different tort than the one the Seventh Circuit just described. Durnell shows up in formula On August 5 the court denied Mead Johnson's motion arguing that the Supreme Court's Roundup preemption decision in Monsanto v. Durnell controls here. In Mead Johnson's version, the Infant Formula Act stands in for the federal labeling scheme at issue there. The denial was without prejudice, which means the argument returns after trial and in every case behind this one. The cross-tort point is the one to keep. Durnell was decided in a herbicide case and is now being run in a food and drug regulatory context within months. Any tort where a federal statute touches the label should expect the same motion. The useful question is how much calendar the motion consumes when it is filed in a thousand cases at once, whether or not it wins. What a verdict does A plaintiff verdict gives the federal docket its first data point and changes the posture of roughly 825 cases plus the state inventory. It would also cut against the read that has developed since the first-wave dismissals, which is that the federal forum is structurally hostile to these claims. A defense verdict makes it four federal failures out of four and leaves plaintiffs with a state-court record that appellate courts have started trimming. The exposure estimates in circulation should be read as ranges rather than figures. Bloomberg Intelligence has put total liability in the low billions; plaintiff-side materials this week cite analyst estimates running from the hundreds of millions to several billion pounds. The gap between those numbers is the same gap the jury is about to address, and neither end of it is a settlement value. What moves that number is whether the second bellwether wave produces a pattern. It also turns on whether the warning-causation record holds up when the next case has a NICU with a donor milk program in it. For where this sits alongside the other dockets moving this year, see the 2026 mass tort map .
